But what would happen if someone could speak every language equally well? Would they be immune to this "mother tongue advantage"?

The researchers tested this idea by using memory tricks to give Dutch participants a temporary second language: Mandarin. The researchers first taught the participants basic Mandarin words and simple sentence structure, and then had them learn lists of word pairs, such as "needle - eye." How to build the best team

Researcher Alex Haslam has developed a simple yet powerful way of building the best performing teams.

Simply have all team members come together to discuss and choose between two topics. These might be the design of team t-shirts, or the process for completing a report.

The topics may be frivolous but the implications are not. People tend to identify as members of groups they choose, rather than those simply assigned to them. The act of choosing therefore helps people to identify with the team.

So, next time you form a team, spend a few moments deciding on something non-work related. This could lead to a positive, identity-based group mentality that builds a sense of belonging and improves group performance.

Why you should use 'you' in your speeches and talks

Want to make your speeches and presentations more engaging? Use the word 'you'.
Speakers often inadvertently use 'I' ('I think', 'I believe') rather than 'you' in their talks. This is fine, to a point, as it shows confidence in the speaker's own opinion, and keeps them in control.
But if used too often it can sound self-obsessed and egotistical. It suggests that the talk is about the speaker, not the people in the audience. If people start feeling like this, they'll start switching off.
So, make sure you use 'you' as often as possible – 'You'll enjoy this next story', 'You can see the evidence', 'You'll be interested to know'.
Remember, it's not all about you. It's all about your listeners!
